book.title: Anger: Wisdom for Cooling the Flames
book.author: Thich Nhat Hanh

confidence_note: Full text not read; potato image and breathing advice come from secondary summaries and quote pages. Old text's three-step list and underlying emotions omitted.
facts: Thich Nhat Hanh compares anger to a potato: a raw potato cannot be eaten.
Mindfulness is the fire that cooks it.
When anger comes up, begin mindful breathing right away; embracing anger and breathing in and out is enough.
Try not to say or do anything while angry.
He also likens anger to garbage that becomes compost and then a flower.
Anger signals something needs taking care of.
tension: Anger cannot be swallowed raw or handed on raw.
opening_idea: A raw potato nobody bites into.

lessons.idea: Let anger cook before serving it.

reflect_final: If something irritated you lately, what would you say differently after two breaths?

use_cases.move: I'm annoyed right now. Give me two breaths and I'll answer properly.
I'd rather not say this raw. Can we talk in ten minutes?
If I write now it goes out uncooked; breathe first, reply after.

pocket_idea: Raw anger is like a raw potato: breathe until it is cooked, then decide what to say.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Anger is a raw potato; it needs the fire of mindfulness before it is edible.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Potato, fire, breathing, not speaking, compost.
